prompt: A cell's output in this course is a plain block of text, while JupyterLab draws the same DataFrame as a shaded table. What differs between the two?
hint: A notebook keeps more than one version of a value.

choices.text: The numbers, because the text version is rounded for printing
choices.why: Both come from the same value; the text is what `print` would show.

choices.text: Only the drawing: the numbers are the same
choices.why: Right. The course shows the `text/plain` version the notebook keeps beside the HTML table.

choices.text: The order of the rows, which the HTML version sorts
choices.why: Neither version reorders anything.

choices.text: The column types, which only the table shows
choices.why: Neither shows the types; lesson 9 asks for them with `dtypes`.

prompt: Why does the course pin every library to an exact version instead of installing the newest?
hint: Think about what a difference between your screen and the page should mean.

choices.text: Newer versions are slower on small data
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Older versions are the only ones that install on Ubuntu
choices.why: The pinned versions are recent ones, and they install on any supported system.

choices.text: So that a different output on your screen means something
choices.why: Right. pandas and NumPy have changed behaviour between versions, so an unpinned difference could be either your code or the library.

choices.text: To keep the virtual environment under 100 MB
choices.why: It is about 650 MB whatever the versions.

prompt: Which path does this course recommend for the lab, and why?
hint: What already keeps the libraries apart from the rest of the computer?

choices.text: A virtual machine, because Python must never be installed on your own computer
choices.why: That is the VM path's argument for somebody who prefers it, not a rule.

choices.text: Online, because it costs nothing
choices.why: It costs your computer nothing and depends on one company's allowance.

choices.text: Installed, because the virtual environment already isolates the libraries
choices.why: Right. The isolation a VM would buy is already there, and JupyterLab runs in the browser you have.

choices.text: Installed, because it is the only path where the outputs match
choices.why: The VM path matches as printed too; the outputs were recorded on Ubuntu 24.04.

prompt: You open a new terminal tomorrow and type `jupyter lab` in `pydata`. What must come before it?
hint: The environment is per terminal.

choices.text: `source .venv/bin/activate`
choices.why: Right. Every new terminal needs the environment activated once.

choices.text: `pip install jupyterlab==4.6.4` again
choices.why: It is still installed; the terminal just does not know where to look.

choices.text: `python3 -m venv .venv` again
choices.why: That would remake the environment; it already exists.

choices.text: `sudo apt-get install -y python3-venv`
choices.why: That is needed once per machine, not per terminal.

prompt: When a terminal has the environment active, the prompt starts with the environment's name in parentheses: `(___)`.
hint: It is the name of the directory you made.

prompt: JupyterLab printed an address ending in `?token=` and a long hexadecimal string. What is the token for?
hint: It changes every time the server starts.

choices.text: It identifies the notebook file to open
choices.why: The address opens the whole application, not one notebook.

choices.text: It is the version of JupyterLab, for bug reports
choices.why: The version is `4.6.4`; `jupyter lab --version` prints it.

choices.text: A password made up for this run, so other programs on the computer cannot use the server
choices.why: Right. Anything that can run code in your kernel is worth protecting.

choices.text: The port the kernel listens on
choices.why: The port is `8888`, before the path.

prompt: `make_data.py` printed how many trips it wrote. How many?
hint: The last of its three numbers.

prompt: Why does the course have you generate the data with a program rather than download a file?
hint: What happens if your file and the course's differ?

choices.text: Downloads are blocked inside a virtual environment
choices.why: A virtual environment blocks nothing; pip downloaded a hundred packages into it.

choices.text: A fixed seed writes the same file on every computer
choices.why: Right. A downloaded file that differed from the course's could not be checked against anything.

choices.text: Generated data has no missing values to worry about
choices.why: These do, on purpose: the bikes that never came back, and six days of rain.

choices.text: Generated files are smaller than any real data set would be
choices.why: Size is not the reason; reproducibility is.

prompt: A row of `trips.csv` has no `ended_at` and no `end_station`. What does it record?
hint: The two missing values go together.

choices.text: A trip still in progress when the file was written
choices.why: The file covers a year that is over; no trip is in progress.

choices.text: A line the program failed to write
choices.why: The program wrote it that way on purpose.

choices.text: A trip that started and ended at the same station
choices.why: That trip would have both values, equal to the start.

choices.text: A bike that never came back to a dock
choices.why: Right, and there are a few of them on purpose.

prompt: In the picture of a notebook as three programs, where do your variables live?
hint: Which of the three runs Python?

choices.text: In the browser tab
choices.why: The page shows outputs; it runs no Python.

choices.text: In the kernel
choices.why: Right. The kernel is the Python process, and its memory is the state.

choices.text: In the `.ipynb` file
choices.why: The file holds sources and outputs, never the variables.

choices.text: In the Jupyter server
choices.why: The server passes code and results along; it does not run them.

prompt: A cell holds `print(lines[1])` and then `lines[1]` on its last line. Why does the second output show `\n` and quotes?
hint: One output is text, the other is a value.

choices.text: Because `print` failed and the notebook showed the raw string instead
choices.why: Both ran; the first output is the print.

choices.text: Because the file was read in binary mode
choices.why: Binary mode would show `b'...'`; this is text.

choices.text: The last line's value is shown as its representation
choices.why: Right: the form Python would accept back as code.

choices.text: Because JupyterLab escapes every string it displays
choices.why: The printed line shows no escapes at all.

prompt: The rain list had six `nan` values, and `len([r for r in rain if r > 0])` counted 167. What happened to the six?
hint: What does a comparison with `nan` return?

choices.text: They raised an error that the comprehension caught
choices.why: A comprehension catches nothing; nothing was raised.

choices.text: `nan > 0` is false, so they dropped out silently
choices.why: Right, and nothing on the screen says so.

choices.text: They were counted as dry days, as if each had a reading of 0 mm
choices.why: They were not counted as anything; `nan` is not 0.

choices.text: `float` turned them into 0.0 when it read an empty field
choices.why: `float('')` fails; the code turned empty fields into `nan` on purpose.

prompt: Match each key, pressed in command mode, to what it does.
hint: One action on the right has no key here.

prompt: What is a `.ipynb` file, on disk?
hint: Open it with `head`.

choices.text: A Python script with comments marking the cells
choices.why: That is what lesson 21 converts it into.

choices.text: A binary snapshot of the kernel's memory
choices.why: The kernel's memory is in no file at all.

choices.text: JSON: cells, sources and saved outputs
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: An HTML page that the browser renders
choices.why: JupyterLab builds the page from the JSON.

prompt: A notebook printed a customer's e-mail in one cell's output. You delete the cell's code and save. Is the address still in the file?
hint: Where does the file keep an output?

choices.text: Yes: outputs are stored apart from the source
choices.why: Right. Clear Outputs of All Cells, then save.

choices.text: No, deleting the code deletes what it printed
choices.why: The output is its own list in the cell; emptying `source` leaves it there.

choices.text: No, outputs are never written to disk
choices.why: They are, under `outputs`.

choices.text: Only while the kernel that printed it is still running
choices.why: The file does not depend on the kernel.

prompt: A notebook arrives with execution counts `7, 3, 12` down the page. What does that tell you?
hint: The counts are the order the kernel ran things in.

choices.text: Some cells failed with an error and were run again later
choices.why: A failed cell still gets a count.

choices.text: It was saved by an older JupyterLab
choices.why: Every version numbers cells the same way.

choices.text: Nine cells were deleted
choices.why: The gaps and the order mean cells ran more than once and out of order; nothing says how many were deleted.

choices.text: They ran out of order, and the outputs reflect that order
choices.why: Right, and lesson 2 is about what that can hide.

prompt: In a `.ipynb`, the key that holds what a cell produced the last time it ran is `___`.
hint: Plural, in English.

prompt: `jupyter lab` answers `bash: jupyter: command not found`, and the prompt has no `(.venv)`. What do you do?
hint: The prompt already told you.

choices.text: Install the `jupyter` package with apt
choices.why: That starts a second JupyterLab whose kernels lack your libraries.

choices.text: Activate the environment in `pydata` and rerun
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Reinstall Python
choices.why: Python is fine; this terminal just has no environment.

choices.text: Run `pip install jupyterlab` without the environment
choices.why: Ubuntu refuses that: `externally-managed-environment`.

prompt: pip printed `2.5.3 Requires-Python >=3.12` and then `Could not find a version`. What is the fix?
hint: An environment belongs to the Python that made it.

choices.text: Install NumPy 2.4.6 instead, the newest the old Python accepts
choices.why: Then your NumPy is not the course's, which is what the pin prevents.

choices.text: Upgrade pip and try again
choices.why: pip found the version; the interpreter is what it refused.

choices.text: Install a newer Python, delete `.venv` and make it again with it
choices.why: Right. An environment cannot change its interpreter in place.

choices.text: Add `--force` to `pip install`
choices.why: There is nothing to force; the package does not support that Python.

prompt: A notebook's `import pandas` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError`, yet `pip list` in your activated terminal shows pandas 3.0.6. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Ask the kernel which Python it is.

choices.text: pandas 3.0.6 is broken on this machine and has to be reinstalled from scratch
choices.why: The terminal imports it fine.

choices.text: The notebook was saved with an old `language_info`
choices.why: That key records the last Python; it does not choose one.

choices.text: pandas needs a restart of the computer after installing
choices.why: No Python library needs that.

choices.text: JupyterLab was started outside the environment, so its kernel is another Python
choices.why: Right. `sys.executable` would not end in `pydata/.venv/bin/python`.

prompt: A second `jupyter lab` says port 8888 is in use and starts on 8889. What is the problem with leaving both?
hint: Each server has its own kernels.

choices.text: The second one cannot save files
choices.why: Both can; that is part of the danger.

choices.text: Two servers with separate kernels: work in one is invisible to the other
choices.why: Right, and both may edit the same notebook file.

choices.text: Port 8889 is blocked by the browser
choices.why: Browsers open any local port.

choices.text: None: two servers share one kernel
choices.why: They never share kernels.

prompt: Put the first-time setup in order.
hint: The environment comes before what goes into it.
items: Check that Python is 3.12 or newer
trap: Installing before activating sends the libraries to the system's Python, which Ubuntu refuses.

prompt: Which of these are saved inside a `.ipynb` file? Choose all that apply.
hint: Variables live in a process.

choices.text: The code of each cell
choices.why: Yes, under `source`.

choices.text: What each cell printed the last time it ran
choices.why: Yes, under `outputs`.

choices.text: The values of the variables
choices.why: No. They are in the kernel and vanish when it stops.

choices.text: The kernel the notebook asks for
choices.why: Yes, under `kernelspec`.

choices.text: The versions of the installed libraries
choices.why: No; only the Python's version is recorded. Lesson 3 adds a file for the rest.

prompt: `weather.csv` has one header line and one line per day of 2025. How many lines does `len(lines)` report?
hint: 2025 was not a leap year.
